Artificial intelligence firm positioned for one of the biggest IPOs in history, with trading slated to begin Thursday
Anthropic set the share price for its debut on the US stock market at $83 on Wednesday, positioning the artificial intelligence company for one of the biggest initial public offerings in history. The firm is slated to begin trading on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT, with CEO Dario Amodei and other co-founders ringing the bell to open the Nasdaq exchange.
The pricing is above Anthropic’s earlier estimates. Last week, the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, set its preliminary share price at $70 to $78. With all shares counted, those prices put Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) from $1.26tn to $1.41tn. Elon Musk’s SpaceX debuted on Wall Street in June with the biggest market offering ever at $1.77tn. With Anthropic setting its share price at $83, it could now surpass SpaceX.
Amodei is planning to sell about $260m worth of shares with the IPO, as are his six fellow co-founders. At the top of the price range, the co-founders’ stakes will be worth more than $18bn each.
When Anthropic filed for its IPO last month, the company detailed rapidly rising revenue in its prospectus: $41m in 2023, $386m in 2024, $4.585bn in 2025 (an increase of more than 1,000%), then $16.286bn in the first six months of 2026 alone. The company disclosed that, as of the end of June, it had raised $141.1bn.
Despite the increasing revenue, Anthropic disclosed a net loss of $80bn for the first half of 2026.
Anthropic’s main expenditure listed in its investor prospectus is computing power from datacenters. The company has compute purchase commitments and lease agreements of more than $70bn over the next 12 months and more than $450bn by 2030, with a further $450bn due by 2045.
Anthropic is the first company at the forefront of the generative AI boom to go public, and its performance is likely to affect investors’ enthusiasm. Its competitor OpenAI was slated to hit Wall Street later this year, but CEO Sam Altman has said that the company opted to delay its IPO until it can overcome safety concerns.
Anthropic’s IPO comes during a volatile time for AI and the stock market. Last month, the industry saw a broader slowdown, with share prices dropping at several companies amid growing concern about the technology. Then, last week, Nvidia, which designs the chips AI companies use to power their chatbots, was racked with a scandal that led to CEO Jensen Huang resigning after reports of multiple extramarital affairs.
texts.https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/18/anthro:
Anthropic has priced its long-awaited IPO at $83 per share , above its initial range of $70 to $78, signaling strong investor appetite for one of the companies at the center of the AI boom, despite market jitters following the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which shook confidence in the industry. The Claude maker sold 980 million shares in the offering, up from the 825 million initially planned, generating $81.3 billion in proceeds and surpassing SpaceX’s $75 billion record to become the largest IPO in history by proceeds raised.
At the IPO price, Anthropic is valued at roughly $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, a significant increase from the $965 billion the company reached in May when it raised $65 billion in its last private market round , but below the $2 trillion it was reportedly aiming for several months ago.
Anthropic will begin its life as a public company on Thursday, trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.” A strong first day of trading would signal that investors remain optimistic about AI adoption, despite recent volatility in AI-driven stocks.
The company’s performance is expected to set expectations for private AI companies, including Anthropic’s main rival OpenAI, which was last reportedly valued at $1.25 billion but has yet to announce plans for an IPO.
Although none of Anthropic’s venture capital investors holds more than a 5% stake in the company, the IPO is a massive windfall for its numerous backers . Investors who own approximately 1% of the company reportedly include Sequoia and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC also holds about a 1% stake in the company, according to a person familiar with the matter. Other backers set to make billions are Iconiq, Menlo Ventures, Coatue, and Sound Ventures, a firm launched by Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, and Spark Ventures, the only VC firm known to hold a board seat at the company.
Some of the company’s existing investors, namely Sequoia, Iconiq, Lightspeed, Accel, and Altimeter Capital Management, are so enthusiastic about Anthropic’s future that they were reportedly planning to buy billions of dollars’ worth of the company’s shares in the IPO.
Yet the investors’ holdings in Anthropic pale in comparison to those of the Claude maker’s strategic partners , Amazon, which owns nearly 15% of the company, and Google, which holds almost 14%. A group of major tech companies, including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC Partners, have also agreed to purchase $26 billion worth of non-voting shares through a private placement alongside the IPO.
The company’s seven co-founders , including CEO Dario Amodei, each sold nearly 3.4 million shares in the IPO, according to the S-1 filing, bringing in about $282 million for each.

Anthropic has raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, leapfrogging SpaceX’s initial $75bn market debut in June.
The San Francisco-based AI giant said in a statement late on Wednesday that the company and its seven co-founders had sold 980 million shares at $83 each.
The bigger-than-expected IPO comes after investor demand for the stock far outstripped forecasts.

Anthropic shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange in New York on Thursday under the ticker “ANT”.

AI-related spending is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner.
Companies betting on the frontier technology currently make up roughly half of the value of the S&P 500 index.

Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang stepped down last week amid unproven claims that a woman he was romantically involved with worked with the Chinese intelligence services.

Ritter said investors are particularly excited about the potential of Anthropic’s AI models to find cures to conditions such as cancer and dementia in the near future.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has quickly become a big name in the tech industry
Anthropic has seen its value jump to as much as $1.5tn (£1.14tn) as its shares are set to start trading on the stock market on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said its shares will be priced at $83 each when it lists on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.
That will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.
Anthropic's stock market debut will make it the first US firm focused exclusively on AI to go public. It will also mark a crucial test for the fast-growing industry, which faces questions over whether the huge amounts of money being poured into the technology will be profitable.
The firm said earlier this month it would offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn.
But demand for Anthropic's stock debut - commonly referred to as its initial public offering, or IPO - is very high, according to one early investor in the company who spoke with the BBC on condition of anonymity.
The person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of the public listing, meaning demand for Anthropic shares exceeded the number of shares available.
If that turns out to be the case, Anthropic's valuation could quickly blow past its target on Thursday when trading begins.
Depending on how strong that demand is, Anthropic could even exceed the early market valuation of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which was the world's most highly valued stock debut when it went public with a value of $2.2tn in June.
However, in the weeks that followed, SpaceX shares fell significantly in price .
As it stands, Anthropic's listing will see the firm raise more than $68bn from its initial investors. It is also expecting another $26bn from private placements. So the total amount the company will raise is expected to be $94bn.
The amount of cash Anthropic has raised from its listing is already more than SpaceX raised in June .
OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year.
Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology, or one that was founded and built around AI tools and products. Its scope is different from tech giants like Google and Microsoft that also develop AI but are involved in other tech services.
The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
There is excitement around Anthropic's listing, but also some concern from investors around its ability to generate revenue and profits going forward.
Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue for Anthropic is whether its business "can keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.
"Nevertheless, it is not an everyday occurrence for public investors to gain direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity," Wang said.
While nearly every other major tech company is pouring huge amounts of money into the technology and infrastructure required for their own AI tools, they are built around social media or online retail or online search. AI tools and applications are secondary.
"Anthropic going public gives us a whole new window into what AI demand looks like," Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC.
Anthropic was started by a group of co-founders , led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, all of whom left their work at OpenAI to start a new AI firm.
The company has carved itself out in the ongoing AI race as more focused on building the technology with safety top of mind.
It refused to comply with a demand by the US Department of Defense that Anthropic's tools be used in an essentially unrestricted way.
CEO Dario Amodei has been outspoken in his belief that AI tools may soon be so powerful that they present a threat to human existence.
The company has urged developers to slow the development of AI, arguing that advanced systems could pose "catastrophic" risks to humanity if they are not handled with appropriate safeguards.
Rival firm OpenAI has also voiced similar concerns about the technology's risks and delayed its plans to list on the stock market to address AI safety concerns.
Nonetheless, Anthropic is looking to grow quickly and gain more access to financing through the public markets in order to do so.
Norton said Anthropic going public now, in a time of market volatility comes down to the simple fact that the company needs access to more money.
"AI is financially demanding," Norton said. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more, and so the time has come."
But broader anxieties have started to grow about the AI industry's business model, which is reliant on expensive computer chips that are in short supply. The technology is also dependent on controversial data centres and funding such operations require deals with other tech companies.
The Federal Reserve Bank has expressed concern about the rapid growth of AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss a potential rate rise.
A few of the meeting's participants also noted that "AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms".
Can Anthropic's record breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?

Pennsylvania records eighth measles death of 2026, a day after the US formally loses its 26-year elimination status.
An unvaccinated resident of Pennsylvania has died after contracting measles, marking the eighth measles-related fatality in the northeastern state this year.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) confirmed the death on Wednesday and said it had been reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
While the department did not publicly identify the individual who died, it said they were a resident of Clinton County, in the centre of the state.
The latest death comes shortly after the United States formally lost its measles elimination status, a designation it held for nearly 26 years.
That status indicated that measles was not endemic to the US, meaning no single strain had circulated continuously for 12 months or more.
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) , a branch of the World Health Organization, updated the US’s designation on Tuesday after reviewing transmission data from the country.
The US is grappling with its worst measles outbreak in more than three decades. As of November 12, the CDC had counted 5,412 confirmed cases since the start of the year.
Pennsylvania, meanwhile, reported 1,589 cases across 46 of its 67 counties. The state’s health agency pledged to continue its aggressive response to the outbreak.
“Approximately 300 DOH staff are proactively working with residents, community organizations, and health care providers to combat the measles outbreak in the Commonwealth through access to fact-based information and access to the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine,” the department wrote in a news release.
The agency also said state health officials have administered more than 11,500 MMR vaccine doses in 2026, including more than 7,200 shots in pop-up clinics since the outbreak erupted in late April.
Experts say vaccine hesitancy in recent decades has contributed to the rising number of cases.
Measles is highly contagious and can spread quickly, particularly when someone coughs or sneezes. The virus can survive for up to two hours in the air, and an estimated 90 percent of those who are not immune will catch it upon exposure, according to medical authorities.
Critics point to leadership under US President Donald Trump as contributing to the measles outbreaks.
One of Trump’s cabinet officials, Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, has questioned the efficacy and safety of vaccines like the MMR shot.
He also said in an interview with NewsNation that the MMR vaccine “contains a lot of aborted foetus debris and DNA particles”, an unsubstantiated claim.
Still, he encouraged vaccination in a social media post on Tuesday, following PAHO’s decision to revoke the US’s measles elimination status.
“We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” he wrote.
The CDC also said it remained committed to stopping measles outbreaks and regaining the country’s elimination status.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC Director Erica Schwartz said.
Before taking office in early 2025, Kennedy claimed that no vaccine was “safe and effective” and promoted the discredited theory that vaccines cause autism.

Trump is stacking the FCC with Republicans, even as the Democrats boycott.
Senate commerce committee Chair Ted Cruz (R-TX) began a meeting Wednesday meant to confirm President Donald Trump’s nominee to the Federal Communications Commission with a lopsided dais. To his right sat all 14 Republican members of the panel, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD). To his left were about a dozen empty chairs — every Democratic member of the panel was absent.
Cruz said he’d learned the night before that Democrats intended to boycott the vote, though Democrats say they’d repeatedly raised their concerns about advancing a Republican FCC nominee without a Democratic one. “The administration has shown it’s willing to move Democrats,” Cruz said, pointing to Senate votes scheduled on bipartisan pairs of nominations to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the Securities and Exchange Commission. And even though the Supreme Court confirmed his power to do so, Cruz said, Trump has not moved to fire any Democrats from the FCC , as he did at the Federal Trade Commission . “This is an ordinary nomination to fill a vacancy previously held by someone in the same party,” Cruz said.
“This is an ordinary nomination to fill a vacancy previously held by someone in the same party”
But in statements and comments to reporters outside the committee room, Democrats said that the process has been far from normal. Senate committees often vote on nominations to historically independent agencies in bipartisan pairs. Confirming Danielle Thumann Severs, senior counsel to FCC Chair Brendan Carr, to become a commissioner at the agency would put the FCC at four total members — three Republicans and one Democrat, Anna Gomez. Gomez’s term has technically expired, though she can remain on the commission through next year unless she’s replaced. But Democrats fear that by confirming a third Republican to the FCC, Trump might finally fire Gomez , because he’d no longer need her present for a quorum to vote on key actions.
Democrats asked for Thumann’s confirmation vote to be withheld until her nomination could be paired with a Democratic nomination. One way to do that would be to renominate Gomez. But so far, the president has not offered any Democratic nominees for the commission. Democrats said they made their concerns clear to Cruz, and added, “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In addition to the procedural concerns, Democrats worry about Thumann’s work as an adviser to Carr, and whether she was truthful about the matters she worked on. In a letter asking Cruz to delay her confirmation vote, Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-NM) detailed his concerns. At the November 10th hearing where Thumann answered committee members’ questions, she testified that she had “not worked with the Chairman on any media-related issues,” Luján noted in the letter. But documents obtained via a Freedom of Information Act request show that Thumann was “looped in” on various media matters, and “helped draft Skydance’s commitments that facilitated the 2 FCC’s approval of the Skydance-Paramount merger,” Luján wrote. “She also played a role in processing informal complaints related to CBS 60 Minutes alleged news distortion and she apparently orchestrated the Commission’s response to consumers regarding the Jimmy Kimmel controversy.” The FCC did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the matter.
Even Cruz admitted concerns with Carr’s handling of Kimmel’s comments in the aftermath of conservative activist Charlie Kirk’s killing. But at Wednesday’s meeting, he said he “emphatically agree[s]” that Thumann had resolved any lingering worries about that. He added that his JAWBONE Act , which the committee previously passed, could directly address First Amendment violations by government agencies of either party. The bill would let individuals sue government officials if they illegally try to compel social media or broadcast companies to remove their speech. Sen. Jerry Moran (R-KS), who’d similarly expressed concern over the Kimmel incident, said he found Thumann’s responses on the subject “comforting,” including in a phone call earlier that morning where he said he’d expressed his “serious interest in how the FCC protects and promotes free speech, including free speech on broadcast.” On the call, he said, “she was able to satisfy me once again in her answers, including an explanation for her role at the FCC and her lack of engagement on this type of issue as the FCC made decisions.”
“If she was lying about this, what else is she lying about and what else is she hiding?”
Speaking to reporters outside of the hearing room ahead of the meeting, Luján accused Thumann of lying to the committee. “The questions that I have is if she was lying about this, what else is she lying about and what else is she hiding?” he said. Luján said he wants both Thumann and Carr to appear before the committee by the end of the year to answer lawmakers’ questions. Asked if he’d support using the committee’s subpoena power or even pursuing impeachment against Carr when Democrats regain power next year, Luján said his vote to confirm Carr as a commissioner under President Joe Biden is among his biggest regrets, and that while he hopes Carr will testify voluntarily, “everything should be on the table here to be able to get answers for the American people.”
When it came time to vote on whether to advance Thumann’s nomination for a final step of a vote on the Senate floor, all 15 Republicans voted “aye.” That gave Thumann enough votes for her nomination to advance to the Senate floor, where it’s expected to pass along party lines once scheduled. Still, the clerk listed off the names of the 13 Democratic committee members whose seats remained empty. There was no response.

The US has hit terrible twin milestones over the past week: Two more people died from measles , bringing this year’s death count to double digits, and the country officially lost its status as a country that had eliminated the highly infectious disease .
The US eliminated measles in 2000 and maintained that status for 26 years. Now, the nation faces an uphill battle to vanquish the virus once more, and it will take years to be measles-free again.
Noel Brewer, a professor of health behavior at the University of North Carolina, presented a report last week to the Pan American Health Organization showing continuous measles transmission for at least 12 months in the US—erasing one of the nation’s greatest public health achievements.
WIRED asked him how he felt after PAHO officials reached a consensus that the country was no longer measles-free. He paused.
“I have not actually thought about my reaction,” he says. After a beat, he says that the loss is “a somber moment for public health” that’s particularly wrenching because it’s a “completely avoidable situation.” Mexico and Canada have managed to wind down their outbreaks, but “measles in America is a runaway train,” Brewer says. “There's no end in sight, and it may even be gaining speed.”
PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa da Silva Jr. officially announced the change in status on Tuesday. “Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” he said at a press conference. “It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization, and death.” Bolivia and Mexico also lost their elimination status this year; Canada lost it a year ago.
Brewer presented three key lines of evidence showing that measles has become endemic in the US. The outbreak in Utah and Arizona has gone on for more than 12 months, and the US has had measles cases every week since January 20, 2025. The genomic data also shows a great deal of similarity across states, indicating the clusters are closely linked—and each week, there are cases where the sources can’t be confirmed, indicating they didn’t come from travel or known contact with other patients.
“We have a problem on our hands,” says William Moss, epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins. And it’s not going away anytime soon. To reclaim its status as measles-free, the US will have to prove it has gone a full year without continued transmission. That’s unlikely to happen under the Trump administration—and its actions have made it more difficult for future leaders.
“Reestablishing elimination is not just about reporting fewer cases—it also requires convincing the world that we have a strong enough surveillance system to find cases and deaths,” Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiologist and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University, tells WIRED in a text.
The fact that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and state health departments differ on how many people have died from measles “is a sign of dysfunction,” Nuzzo says. There have been 10 confirmed measles deaths so far this year—seven in Pennsylvania, two in Wisconsin, and one in New York—but the CDC only lists six.
Such chaos also breeds distrust, says Frederic Bertley, president and CEO of the Center of Science and Industry. That's “a huge problem” for a public trying to parse who is telling the truth and whether they should listen, he says.
Even as measles was eliminated, anti-vaccine rhetoric began to rise , especially around the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine. Vaccination rates began falling—spurred in part by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an environmental lawyer turned anti-vaccine activist who published a now-retracted article alleging a link between vaccines and autism in 2005. He continued crusading against vaccines as head of Children’s Health Defense and at the helm of the Department of Health and Human Services during President Donald Trump’s second term.
The Trump administration has done little to stop the outbreaks, cutting billions in funding from state, local, territorial, and tribal public health departments and offering conflicting messages on vaccines. During a televised February 2025 cabinet meeting following the first child death in a decade, Kennedy said “it's not unusual, we have measles outbreaks every year.” The CDC hasn’t held a single press conference on measles throughout the entire outbreak; as PAHO was making its measles status announcement on Tuesday, HHS sent out an email about Kennedy’s cooking show.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC director Erica Schwartz said in a statement . “Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.” Kennedy posted on X , “I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”
To regain its elimination status, the US needs to address barriers to health care access, missed vaccination opportunities, misinformation, and vaccine hesitancy, Barbosa said. That includes mounting wide-reaching vaccination campaigns, expanding laboratory testing capacity, and responding quickly to cases, including contact tracing. It’s the bread and butter of public health, but the longer it takes to create a comprehensive response, the more it will cost, experts warn.
Future efforts to contain measles will require “a stronger centralized federal response to these outbreaks” paired with support for “very local responses,” says Moss. That means identifying communities with long-standing under-vaccination and understanding why, he says, as well as improving trust in public health guidance.
“Immunity gaps” tend to concentrate in specific geographic areas and communities, and national or even state-level data can “mask these significant inequalities, providing an incomplete picture of the population's actual level of protection,” Barbosa said.
The CDC announced $100 million in August and September—more than a year after the outbreak began—to help fund state and regional efforts to combat measles, but Congress will need to allocate $100 million to $400 million more for measles elimination in coming months, Brewer says.
“More than 90 percent of children get the measles vaccine, Brewer points out. “This is a vaccine that has extraordinary public support, and it goes across the aisle.”
But to achieve herd immunity, vaccination rates need to be at least 95 percent due to how contagious the disease is. High transmissibility also means measles is very hard to uproot once it begins to spread.
Yet ending national measles transmission is “its own reward,” Brewer says. It spares children’s lives, keeps them out of hospitals, and prevents blindness and other lifelong complications. “We no longer have that benefit,” he says. “Children are now being stalked by this incurable and deadly disease.”

Measles became endemic in the US months ago—and it’s only accelerating.
International health authorities formally announced on Tuesday that the US has lost its measles elimination status, a hard-fought public health triumph won in 2000 after decades-long vaccination efforts. The loss had been widely expected by public health experts for months, and the decision was leaked by the press last week. Still, having the designation officially stripped stings.
After the announcement Tuesday, public health experts, doctors, and political leaders decried the dramatic backslide for the US, calling it “ shameful ” and a “ national embarrassment .” News articles point to the staggering vertical rise of measles cases this year, currently over 5,400 cases , more than any other year since 1991. An explosive measles outbreak in Pennsylvania accounts for over 1,500 of those cases . There have been 10 confirmed deaths across three states, several deaths just in the last week.
But the measles data that caused the US to lose its status—the bits of it that are public at least—paint a darker picture of where the US is in its rematch with measles, the most contagious virus known on Earth. For one thing, almost none of the data from this year—the cases, the explosive Pennsylvania outbreak, the deaths—factored in to the loss. It was lost earlier. What’s happening now is a runaway epidemic.
The US measles elimination status is a designation granted by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which is a regional division of the World Health Organization. Last week a committee of experts assembled by the PAHO, called the RVC, met to review measles data for countries across the region, including the US. (RVC is short for the Measles, Rubella and Congenital Rubella Syndrome Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission.)
For their review of the US data, the RVC heard from an independent committee of experts from the US, called the NSC, which presented measles data collected from January 2025 onward. (The NSC is short for the US National Sustainability Committee for the Elimination of Measles, Rubella, and Congenital Rubella Syndrome.)
According to the PAHO, an elimination status is lost when epidemiological and laboratory data shows that a single viral lineage has spread continuously for at least 12 months within a country. At this point, the virus is considered to be reestablished or endemic. So, to withdraw the US elimination status, the RVC needed to see evidence that a single introduction of a measles virus led to a 12-month-long chain of cases, which requires a lot of data.
The full set of data the NSC presented to the RVC is private for now. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention needs to review and approve such data for public release, which can be a lengthy process that has not yet occurred.
The Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the CDC, did not respond to a question from Ars Technica regarding when the data may be released.
But Ars Technica spoke with the chair of the NSC, Noel Brewer, who tried to talk through the pieces of data in the NSC report to the PAHO that he could discuss—these are pieces that have already been made public at some point by others, such as by state health officials or researchers. Brewer said the NSC presented the PAHO with genetic data spanning January 2025 to January 2026, and also epidemiological data that extended to June 2026.
In a press briefing Tuesday, officials for the PAHO made clear that only some of the data presented by NSC factored into its assessment of the US elimination status. The RVC only looked at the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, which doesn’t include the massive outbreak ongoing in Pennsylvania, which began in April. “The number of cases in Pennsylvania did not actually contribute to the decision that was made by the Reverification Commission,” Rhonda Sealey-Thomas, PAHO’s assistant director, explicitly told reporters Tuesday. For 2025, the US reported 2,289 cases nationally.
Still, there was no ambiguity about the US losing its status; “multiple lines of data show clearly that the US has sustained transmission of measles,” Brewer told Ars.
Brewer, who is also the Gillings Distinguished Professor in Public Health at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, confirmed that the beginning of the end of US elimination was January 20, 2025, in Texas —that date was included in the letter PAHO sent to the US informing it of the loss of elimination status. That Texas outbreak was declared over on August 18, 2025, after 762 cases were confirmed in the state. But the virus carried on elsewhere and is still simmering.
“Since January 20, 2025, the US, Canada, and Mexico have been passing measles cases back and forth across borders,” Brewer said, and the national data shows multiple, “genetically distinct” measles introductions into the US. “However, there is one genomic lineage that predominates across the cases and ties many of them, the majority of them, together,” he said.
For people closely tracking the US measles status, a key question has been whether the big outbreaks that followed the initial one in Texas were clearly linked. If they were, it would be immediately obvious that the US had lost the elimination status; but if not, and the outbreaks were driven by different virus introductions, the US could have kept its measles-free status based on the technicality of how the status is defined.
Data that might hold the answer to this question has been elusive. The measles strain in Texas, D8-9171, appeared similar to the viruses seen subsequently in big outbreaks in Arizona and Utah . But the strain was also similar to those from Mexico and Canada. Generally, there can be relatively small genetic changes among measles viruses, and genetic data alone is not used by PAHO to evaluate elimination. In June, ProPublica tried to get at the answer itself, conducting its own genetic analysis of measles strains in the US. It concluded that “the measles virus still spreading in Utah as of this May is very closely related to the one that sickened Texans over a year ago.” But the outlet acknowledged this wasn’t a “smoking gun.”
To date, the question lingers. Brewer cannot yet explicitly disclose what the NSC reported to the PAHO about possible links between the Texas outbreak and any of the subsequent large outbreaks in 2025. That includes the one in nearby Utah or one in South Carolina, which began in October 2025 and ultimately tallied 997 cases by the time it was declared over in April 2026.
For its part, the PAHO did not respond to multiple requests for comment from Ars Technica on linkages between the outbreaks.
But in a twist, Brewer noted that the answer to the question might be moot; the lineage that started in Texas on January 20 might not be the only one that has been sustained and could have lost the country its status. There are “one or two that have gone on for more than 12 months,” he said.
With the designation now formally lost, health and medical experts are coming to grips with the reality that measles is once again endemic in the US. Details of how the US should move forward are up for debate; the US is now required to submit a “corrective action plan” to the PAHO, outlining how the country intends to regain its elimination status. But the fundamental solution is obvious and straightforward: The US needs to increase vaccination rates.
While the virus has been raging in religious communities with low vaccination rates, the entire US has seen slipping vaccination coverage. That makes it easier for the virus to gain a foothold virtually anywhere.
A protective vaccination rate is considered to be 95 percent; according to the latest data , only 92.4 percent of kindergartners were vaccinated with the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year. Only 10 states have MMR vaccination rates at or above the 95 percent threshol…

Democrats try to prevent quorum, say Thumann lied about not working on media issues.
A Senate committee chaired by Ted Cruz (R-Texas) voted today to approve a Federal Communications Commission nominee, despite accusations that the nominee gave false testimony about her work as a legal advisor for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. Democrats attempted to prevent a quorum by not showing up, but Cruz proceeded with a Republican-only vote.
All 15 Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted to approve Trump nominee Danielle Thumann, while the committee’s 13 Democrats were absent. “We’re going to be doing our job today, even if the Democrats refuse to show up to do theirs,” Cruz said at today’s hearing.
Nominees are vetted in committees first, and then seek require majority approval from the Senate. Republicans are hoping to get Thumann confirmed before Democrats take Senate control in January.
Although the Senate Commerce Committee generally requires one minority member to be present for nomination votes, a spokesperson for Cruz said Senate rules allow the nomination to be advanced for a vote in the entire chamber. A spokesperson for Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), the top Democrat on the committee, said in response that “since 2005, Commerce Committee rules required that a quorum include one member of the minority for official action on bill, resolution, or nomination.”
Technically, the committee has operated with no rules during Cruz’s chairmanship because Cruz “failed to pass committee rules” for the current session of Congress, Cantwell’s spokesperson said. “Nevertheless, in practice it has operated in line with rules from the last Congress (and this provision, specifically, since 2005), including that a quorum with a member of the minority party must be present for official action on a nomination or legislation. Until today.”
At a hearing last week, Thumann said she never worked with Carr on media-related topics, leading to accusations that she provided false testimony. “I have not worked with the chairman on any media-related issues,” Thumann said after Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) asked, “Do you support Chairman Carr’s illegal campaign to remove Jimmy Kimmel from the nation’s airwaves?”
“It appears that Ms. Thumann misled the Committee and offered false testimony, seriously calling into question her judgment and character and impeding the Committee’s work in determining whether she should be seated on the Commission,” Luján wrote in a letter to Cruz yesterday. “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media-related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount.”
The FCC website describes Thumann as senior counsel to Carr on matters before the Wireline Bureau, the Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau, and the Consumer and Governmental Affairs Bureau. Emails obtained in a public records request by the group Protect Democracy show she had some involvement in media-related matters.
Thumann provided follow-up responses to senators’ questions this week. She said that her work sometimes includes “reviewing documents or filings in a matter outside of my designated portfolio. However, I did not have any conversations with Paramount, CBS, or Skydance related to the merger.”
Thumann has been referred to as Thumann Severs in the nomination process, but she uses the name Thumann.
Luján wrote that Thumann “played a role in processing informal complaints related to” alleged news distortion on CBS’s 60 Minutes , and that “she apparently orchestrated the Commission’s response to consumers regarding the Jimmy Kimmel controversy.” However, Thumann was only a recipient of the Kimmel-related emails we found in a search of the messages.
The emails do show that Thumann approved language used in a response the FCC gave to complaints about the alleged news distortion in a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris. The response informed people who submitted complaints that they should instead submit comments on an FCC docket that had been set up for the 60 Minutes proceeding.
“Hi Kristi, I have confirmed with the Chairman and Erin that we would like for complainants to be encouraged to resubmit their news distortion complaints in the relevant ECFS [Electronic Comment Filing System] proceeding,” Thumann wrote. “Can you please work on some draft language to send to consumers that would advise them on this step (including how to use ECFS)?”
Democrats announced yesterday that they would try to prevent a quorum for today’s vote. They objected to adding a third Republican to the committee while a Democratic seat remains empty.
“All Democratic members of the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee object to the majority stacking independent commissions with Republicans and rushing nominees through the Committee process in this lame duck session with no Democratic pairs,” Cantwell said in a statement.
Cantwell and other Democrats on the committee sent a letter to Cruz urging him to cancel the vote, while quoting his own words from 2014. “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the Democratic committee members said.
Cruz said today that “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January. But today is November 18.” Cruz said there is “ample precedent” for advancing nominations in a lame-duck session.
Senate Commerce Committee rules state that a quorum for nomination votes requires a “majority of the members, which includes at least one minority member.” But a Cruz spokesperson pointed to certain clauses regarding committee quorums in Senate rules when contacted by Ars today.
In the Standing Rules of the Senate , paragraph 7 of rule XXVI says that “no measure or matter or recommendation shall be reported from any committee unless a majority of the committee were physically present,” and does not have any requirement for minority members to be present. Elsewhere, the Senate rules say that when a committee reports a measure to the Senate floor, “no point of order shall lie with respect to that measure” as long as the committee took its action “in conformity with the requirements of paragraph 7 of rule XXVI.”
While committees can have different quorum rules, a Cruz spokesperson said this functions as a “cleansing clause” so that “earlier procedural irregularities, such as a violation of a committee rule, cannot be used to invalidate the vote on the Senate floor.”
FCC nominations have traditionally been paired with one Republican and one Democrat when there is an empty seat for each party. But Cruz said that’s not a requirement.
“There’s nothing that requires the president to nominate in pairs… the law merely says that no more than three of the commissioners may be from the same party,” Cruz said during the Republican-only meeting.
The Communications Act prohibits a single party from holding more FCC seats than is necessary to form a majority. It says, “The maximum number of commissioners who may be members of the same political party shall be a number equal to the least number of commissioners which constitutes a majority of the full membership of the Commission.”
Republicans would have a 3-1 majority on the FCC if Thumann is confirmed by the Senate. The sole Democrat, Anna Gomez, would have to leave at the end of 2027 if Trump does not nominate her for another term.
“There is no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks… Ms. Thumann Severs’ nomination should be postponed until the next Congress and paired with Commissioner Gomez’s renomination and the nomination of an additional Democratic commissioner,” Democrats told Cruz in their letter this week.

Şirketin geçici Üst Yöneticisi (CEO) Colette Kress, daha önce ABD yönetiminin ihracat izni verdiği Hopper serisi veri merkezi işlemcilerinin artık Çin'e gönderilmediğini bildirdi. Söz konusu karar, Nvidia'nın Çin pazarındaki geleceğine ilişkin soru işaretlerini artırırken ABD ile Çin arasındaki yarı iletken rekabetini de yeniden gündeme taşıdı.
Nvidia'nın açıklaması, şirketin 17 Kasım'da gerçekleştirdiği mali sonuç toplantısında geldi. Kress, 25 Ekim'de sona eren çeyrekte Çin'e lisans kapsamında 2,4 milyar dolar değerinde Hopper serisi ürün satıldığını, ancak gelecek döneme ilişkin sevkiyat beklentilerinde Çin'e yönelik bu ürünlere yer verilmediğini söyledi.
Kress, şirketin artık Çin'e lisanslı Hopper veri merkezi ürünleri göndermediğini belirtirken kararın gerekçesine veya sevkiyatların ne zaman yeniden başlayabileceğine ilişkin ayrıntı paylaşmadı. Dolayısıyla Nvidia'nın bu adımının kalıcı bir satış yasağı mı yoksa mevcut koşullara bağlı bir sevkiyat durdurma kararı mı olduğu henüz bilinmiyor.
Nvidia'nın açıklaması, Çin'e yönelik bütün ürün satışlarının sona erdiği anlamına gelmiyor. Karar, özellikle Hopper ailesindeki veri merkezi ürünlerini kapsıyor. Bu ailenin en önemli işlemcilerinden biri olan H200, yapay zeka modellerinin eğitilmesi ve çalıştırılmasında kullanılıyor. Şirketin daha düşük kapasiteli ve ihracat kurallarına uygun bazı ürünleri içinse farklı bir tablo söz konusu.
Nvidia'nın son kararı, tek başına alınmış bir şirket kararından çok daha büyük bir mücadelenin parçası. ABD'nin Çin'in gelişmiş yarı iletkenlere erişimini sınırlandırması, Pekin'in yabancı teknolojiye bağımlılığı azaltma politikası ve iki ülkenin yapay zeka alanında üstünlük kurma çabası, bugünkü tablonun oluşmasında etkili oldu.
Üstelik Washington ve Pekin'in Nvidia çiplerine yönelik politikaları her zaman aynı yönde ilerlemedi. ABD bazı işlemcilerin ihracatına izin verirken Çin yönetimi aynı ürünlerin ülkeye girişini sınırlandırdı. Bu durum, Nvidia'yı iki farklı düzenleyici sistemin arasında bıraktı.
ABD, Çin'in gelişmiş yarı iletkenlere ve bu çipleri üretmek için kullanılan teknolojilere erişimini sınırlandırmak amacıyla Ekim 2022'de kapsamlı ihracat kontrolleri uygulamaya başladı. Washington yönetiminin temel gerekçesi, gelişmiş işlem gücünün Çin ordusu tarafından kullanılabilecek yapay zeka sistemlerinin geliştirilmesini kolaylaştırmasıydı.
Kısıtlamalar, Nvidia'nın A100 ve H100 gibi yüksek performanslı veri merkezi işlemcilerini de etkiledi. Şirket, Çin pazarındaki faaliyetlerini sürdürebilmek için ABD'nin belirlediği teknik eşiklere uygun, performansı sınırlandırılmış ürünler geliştirmek zorunda kaldı.
Washington, Ekim 2023'te kuralları güncelleyerek yalnızca işlem gücünü değil, çiplerin bellek bant genişliği ve işlem yoğunluğu gibi teknik özelliklerini de kapsayan yeni sınırlamalar getirdi. Böylece şirketlerin mevcut kuralları aşmak için daha düşük performanslı işlemciler tasarlaması da zorlaştı.
Nvidia'nın Çin pazarı için geliştirdiği H20 işlemcisi, ABD'nin ihracat kurallarına uyum sağlamak amacıyla performansı sınırlandırılmış ürünlerden biriydi. Ancak ABD yönetimi Nisan 2025'te bu işlemcinin Çin'e ihracatı için de lisans zorunluluğu getirdi.
Kararın ardından Nvidia, satılamayan H20 ürünleri ve üretim taahhütleri nedeniyle 2026 mali yılının ilk çeyreğinde 4,5 milyar dolarlık gider kaydetti. ABD yönetimi Ağustos 2025'te bazı Çinli müşterilere H20 gönderilmesine izin veren lisanslar verse de bu kez Çin yönetiminin kısıtlamaları devreye girdi. Nvidia'nın mali raporlarına göre şirket, Çin'in kendi sınırlandırmaları nedeniyle bu ürünlerin tamamını satamadı.
Bu gelişme, Nvidia'nın Çin pazarında karşılaştığı sorunun yalnızca ABD'nin ihracat politikalarıyla sınırlı olmadığını gösterdi. Şirket bir taraftan Washington'ın belirlediği teknik sınırları aşmadan ürün geliştirmeye çalışırken diğer taraftan Pekin'in yerli çip üreticilerini destekleyen politikalarıyla karşı karşıya kaldı.
ABD ile Çin arasındaki gerilime rağmen Donald Trump yönetimi, Aralık 2025'te Nvidia'nın H200 işlemcilerinin belirli Çinli müşterilere satılmasına izin verileceğini duyurdu. Bu karar, Nvidia'nın Çin pazarına yeniden erişebilmesi açısından önemli bir gelişmeydi.
ABD Ticaret Bakanlığına bağlı Sanayi ve Güvenlik Bürosu (BIS), 13 Ocak 2026'da ihracat lisanslarının değerlendirilmesine ilişkin politikasını değiştirdi. Daha önce reddedilme ihtimali esas alınarak değerlendirilen bazı gelişmiş işlemciler için artık belirli güvenlik koşullarının sağlanması durumunda başvuru bazında inceleme yapılabilecekti.
Bu düzenleme yalnızca Nvidia H200 işlemcisini değil, AMD'nin MI325X modeli gibi benzer özelliklere sahip ürünleri de kapsıyordu.
İzin, koşulsuz bir satış serbestisi anlamına gelmiyordu. ABD yönetiminin belirlediği şartlar arasında Çin'e gönderilecek ürünlerin ABD'deki müşterilere ayrılan küresel üretim kapasitesini azaltmaması, Çinli alıcıların ihracat kurallarına uyum ve müşteri denetimi için yeterli güvenlik prosedürlerine sahip olması, çiplerin sevkiyat öncesinde ABD'de bağımsız bir kuruluş tarafından teknik ve güvenlik testlerinden geçirilmesi ve ihracatın belirlenen performans ve güvenlik sınırları içinde kalması bulunuyordu.
H200 satışları için getirilen bir diğer dikkat çekici koşul ise yüzde 25'lik gümrük tarifesiydi. Çiplerin Çin'e gönderilmeden önce ABD'ye ithal edilmesi ve gerekli denetimlerden geçirilmesi öngörülüyordu. Bu süreç, satışın maliyetini ve lojistik koşullarını da değiştirdi.
Böylece ABD, Nvidia'nın Çin'e tamamen sırtını dönmesini istemeyen ticari yaklaşımı ile gelişmiş işlem gücünün Çin'in askerî ve stratejik kapasitesini artırabileceği yönündeki güvenlik kaygılarını aynı politikada buluşturmaya çalıştı. Ancak bu kez de Pekin'in onayı ve yerli üreticileri önceleyen politikası, planlanan satışların önünde engel oluşturdu.
ABD'nin H200 satışlarına izin vermesi, Çinli teknoloji şirketlerinin bu işlemcilere kolayca erişebileceği anlamına gelmedi. Çin yönetimi, Nvidia'nın gelişmiş işlemcilerine yönelik ithalatı sınırlandırarak yerli yarı iletken üreticilerini desteklemeye yönelik politikasını sürdürdü.
Reuters'ın Ocak 2026'da yayınladığı habere göre Çinli gümrük yetkililerine H200 işlemcilerinin ülkeye girişine izin verilmediği bildirildi. Aynı dönemde Çinli teknoloji şirketlerinin temsilcileri de hükûmet yetkilileriyle toplantılara çağrıldı. Şirketlere, zorunlu olmadıkça H200 satın almamaları yönünde talimat verildiği aktarıldı.

MyMems, from the creator of SimCity and The Sims, is a new social simulator powered by AI.
Will Wright, the creator of legendary franchises like SimCity and The Sims , is working on a new game — and it’s built around AI. The new title, focused on your memories, is called MyMems . Like Wright’s other titles, it sounds extremely ambitious, giving players a new way to explore worlds they create on their own. “We want to take your autobiography and turn it into a toy world,” he tells The Verge .
The MyMems website describes the mobile game as a “social simulation” with worlds “built from your memories and the people who shaped you.” You can add “memories” to your game, like speaking a short story to your phone, and those memories are generated into pieces you can place on the game’s map. Your worlds can also include AI-powered avatars, which can represent people you know in your life. Ideally, as you play, the planet starts to become a “map of your psyche,” kind of like Inside Out , Wright says. Worlds can be private, but you can also share them with others.
Here’s another way to think of it, from Virginia McArthur, executive producer and GM at MyMems developer Gallium Studios: “It’s a cozy world builder with a really deep social simulation underneath.”
I’ll admit that I don’t totally get it, and it seems like a tricky idea to grasp without playing it. Still, as heady of a concept as it might be — turning your memories into a game world — Wright and team still want it to be fun. “This isn’t meant to be your legacy diary necessarily,” says Anthony Maitz, a product manager at Gallium Studios. “It’s meant to just be something you kind of play around with.” However, Maitz notes that what you’re working toward is a “proxy” of you — a word that seems to be the inspiration of the game’s earlier title, Proxi: Yesterday’s You Tomorrow . The game will use the “Behavior Engine” from a company called Artificial Agency , which makes AI tech for video games, as a “foundational technology.”
Like other industries, gaming is starting to reckon with generative AI. Early AI virtual worlds created with models from a startup backed by a Pixar cofounder and Google’s Project Genie weren’t experiences you’d actually want to spend dedicated time with, and indie developers I spoke to in March were largely opposed to the technology . But AI technology has taken some big leaps this year with companies like Google , Meta , and Roblox now letting users make games with AI right from their phone, and retro gaming becoming overrun with AI-powered ports of classic titles.
Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said earlier this year that generative AI has “zero part in what Rockstar Games is building” with GTA VI . But even as a recent industry survey indicated that more game developers are starting to use generative AI as part of their job , workers are pushing back against generative AI use , and the technology is at the center of fierce debates over indie game awards .
Many players are rejecting AI outright, and I wondered if the Gallium Studios team was worried about opposition toward MyMems ’ use of AI. Wright says he has three boys at home and that they are all “pretty negative” on AI. He attributes negativity over AI to be toward the meaning of art and authorship and credit, a concern he calls “well-founded.” But he also calls AI an “amazing tool.”
“We’re not making slop,” says McArthur. But Maitz notes that while the team has “been concerned” about a negative response to the generative AI use, they’ve learned that people don’t mind when they use AI in a “ Scribblenauts -y style” for things like having the game make a high school. The team also found that people got “addicted” to a test app with a character creator, including Maitz’s own daughter, who he says “hates” AI. “By making it so that the player is authoring it over and over, bit by bit, it doesn’t really feel like you cheated,” Maitz says.
MyMems , which is set to launch in 2027, will join a growing field of other social simulations, like Krafton’s Inzoi and Nintendo’s smash hit Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream . But none quite have the pull of The Sims , which remains one of EA’s most important franchises. With The Sims , Wright says that many people tried making their real families in the game.
“It was interesting how people really were naturally trying to map this game, which was like a little toy, onto their real life,” he says. With MyMems , that’s what the team is trying to do the “follow-through” on — what if they made the whole game focused on you?
Imagine opening a family scrapbook and the way people and things jump out, Wright explains. “As you go through more and more pages, pretty soon you have this whole little circus of people and events and things from your life.” It’s chaos, he says. “I want something that feels kind of like that.”

With MyMems , Wright says he wants to “turn the simulation inward.”
The computer gaming world hasn’t heard much from Will Wright ( SimCity , The Sims ) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright’s subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA . Now, well over 15 years later, Wright is starting to promote his next digital simulation, which will use generative AI technology to craft a game-like experience from players’ memories.
MyMems , which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright’s previous projects by “turn[ing] the simulation inward,” as Wright’s Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning . The game will mine memories provided by the player to create digital people that can then form teams to solve puzzles in the game world.
“If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?” Wright says by way of example in the release. “If I had to build a bridge across a short chasm, which three people from my life would I choose to help me?”
In an accompanying announcement video , Wright talks about how the “plausible behavior” in a game like The Sims still didn’t effectively capture the nuances of people he encounters in real life. “It was nowhere near them understanding my claustrophobia or why my sister and I fought so much… We’re actually taking parts of your life, your memories, your experiences, people you know, and turning that into a game that’s very personal.”
Wright said MyMems will be able to extract generalized themes from your memories into self-contained areas that Wright compared to the various parts in a theme park: Sports, vacations, injuries, memories, and deaths could all be the basis for their own zones to play in. Players will also have the option to create worlds based on shared memories with family, friends, and co-workers, for example.
Since this is 2026, it shouldn’t be surprising that MyMems is making heavy use of generative AI (with a “proprietary behavior engine” on top) to transform your typed-up memories into simulated locales and characters. In the announcement video, Wright praises the “entirely open-ended” AI systems Gallium is using “to extract from the stories and whatnot based upon the memories you put into the game.”
But Wright’s focus on mining memories for simulation content predates the current generative AI boom. What has now become MyMems started off as Proxi , a mobile simulation that was first announced in 2018 as “a game of self-discovery, a game where we actually uncover the hidden you.” But after years of pre-production work (as outlined in an excellent Vulture piece earlier this year ), Wright’s Gallium Studios finally ran out of funding in late 2024, leading to mass layoffs for the small team and an uncertain future for the project.
Now the idea has been revived thanks in large part to a partnership with AI middleware firm Artificial Agency . Until now, that company has mainly been focused on agentic systems that can create “virtual players” to playtest a game or serve as a partner for human players.
Now, Artificial Agency’s marketing says the company’s AI tool will be used to create “a personal behavior model and a knowledge graph” from players’ memories, drawing some unsettling comparisons to big tech surveillance.
“Meta knows what you click,” the company writes. “Netflix knows what you watch. Nobody knows what you remember. MemDNA learns from your memories locally and only with your permission.”
Wright said the partnership with Artificial Agency will let Gallium benefit from “off-the-shelf” AI solutions without having to “become an AI research company” in its own right. He also said the collaboration will help limit costs by providing a cheaper option than the “really expensive” frontier models that might be overkill for a project like this.
“Right now AI has opened a vast new design area and I’m enjoying, you know, exploring that as a designer,” Wright said.

Nvidia , Çin pazarına yönelik stratejisinde önemli bir değişikliğe gidiyor. Şirketin geçici CEO'su Colette Kress , Nvidia'nın artık Çin'e lisanslı Hopper mimarili veri merkezi ürünleri göndermediğini açıkladı . Bu kapsamda şirketin H200 yapay zeka çiplerinin Çin'e sevkiyatı da sona ermiş oldu.

Aynı gün Nvidia, ulusal güvenlik politikaları, ihracat kontrollerine uyum ve küresel ticaret risklerini takip edecek yönetim kurulu seviyesinde yeni bir komite kurduğunu da duyurdu .
Hatırlatmak gerekirse ABD Başkanı Donald Trump , geçtiğimiz yılın aralık ayında Nvidia'nın H200 çiplerini belirli Çinli müşterilere satmasına izin vermişti . Bloomberg'ün paylaştığı bilgilere göre Nvidia, yalnızca 2026'nın üçüncü çeyreğinde Çin'e yaklaşık 2,4 milyar dolarlık Hopper mimarili veri merkezi ürünü sattı. Jensen Huang, ABD'nin gelişmiş yapay zeka çiplerinin Çin'e satışını kısıtlayan politikalarına uzun süredir karşı çıkıyordu. Huang, Çin pazarını tamamen yerel üreticilere bırakmanın ABD teknoloji sektörü açısından olumsuz sonuçlar doğurabileceğini savunuyordu. Nvidia'nın yeni yönetimi altında alınan son karar ise şirketin bu yaklaşımından uzaklaşmaya başladığına işaret ediyor.
Nvidia'nın kararı, ABD'nin Çin'in gelişmiş yapay zeka çiplerine erişimini sınırlamak amacıyla getirdiği yeni düzenlemelerle aynı döneme denk geliyor. ABD Ticaret Bakanlığı'nın açıkladığı yeni kurallar , Çinli şirketlerin yurt dışındaki veri merkezleri üzerinden gelişmiş ABD çiplerinden yararlanmasını da zorlaştırıyor. Paylaşılan bilgilere göre; yatırım bankası Jefferies, söz konusu ihracat kurallarının gelecek yıl Nvidia'nın veri merkezi gelirlerinde 44 ila 62 milyar dolar arasında kayba yol açabileceğini tahmin ediyor. Nvidia'nın H200 satışlarını sonlandırması, Jensen Huang'ın ayrılışının ardından şirketin Çin politikasındaki ilk önemli değişikliklerden biri olarak öne çıkıyor. Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B , RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles . We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.
We are releasing BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 checkpoints for everyone to try and build on. In this post, we explain how carefully designed tasks and efficient infrastructure made these gains possible on a limited compute budget.
DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above 1 . The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, a notoriously hard long-horizon benchmark. Our magic lies in the following three key ingredients: high-quality training data, efficient training backend, and robust sandboxes.
We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI , starting from Eigent AI’s large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 of them made it into the final training set. The training tasks are selected based on three criteria.
RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.
57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU's peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.
2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.
Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.
During training, every attempt the agent makes runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task's environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded. All of the RadixArk team's work on this release ran in sandboxes on our own service, built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, the service ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running at the same time.
Reliable as it grew. The service grew from a single machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all of them while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded, and since late October more than 99.95% have. Getting there took a steady stream of fixes and improvements, such as keeping a machine from freezing when it runs out of memory.
80% lower cost. Our cloud infrastructure cost for the project's sandboxes was about 80% lower than the cost of running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to give each sandbox memory that grows and shrinks with what it actually uses. A sandbox usually uses only a small part of the memory it asks for, so each machine can run many more sandboxes.
You can download DaisyRose-27B from Hugging Face , and you can train your own agents with our open source reinforcement learning framework Miles .
DaisyRose-27B is one example of what high-quality data and efficient infrastructure can make possible. We are bringing this approach to teams building specialized models, with a focus on improving the capabilities they need while preserving the model’s broader strengths. If you are exploring post-training for your own model, reach out at contact@radixark.ai .
We are deeply grateful to Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and to the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B, the foundation of our work. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, as well as other open-source projects, including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.
How we evaluated: Terminal Bench 4.1 is averaged over 8 runs per task, using our internal mini-swe-agent harness with summarization turned on. Terminal Bench 2.1 is averaged over 5 runs per task, using the Terminus 2 harness. DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE Bench Pro v2 are averaged over 8 and 5 runs per task, both using the mini-swe-agent harness. HLE (text-only) is averaged over 5 runs per problem, graded by GPT-6 Luna, with no tools. IFBench is averaged over 4 runs on each of its 300 prompts, scored by the official allenai/IFBench scorer as prompt-level loose accuracy on the final response, with the thinking left out. GPQA Diamond is averaged over 8 runs on each of its 198 questions, using the simple-evals multiple-choice template and answer extraction, with the answer order reshuffled on every run. ↩

Bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows.
Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows.
Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index , Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index . Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing.
The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window.
Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app .
Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench .
Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI , ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions.
On scientific and mathematical reasoning, spanning quantitative analysis, mathematics, and technical research problems, Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%).
Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. It cuts down on redundant file reads, shares progress as it works, and handles context compaction reliably in long sessions.
Across core developer and researcher workflows, Neon achieves frontier performance and is competitive with the leading models in its class, ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), with a score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0 . For production-ready code, Neon handles multi-file debugging and refactoring across repositories with targeted, surgical edits. On SWE-sweep, it already leads on the mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity showing what the Antigravity harness unlocks.
Driving Blender MCP in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon used /swarm to build a photorealistic 3D lab bench visualizing the model names with elemental accuracy pairing Bunsen flames for Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen with high-voltage gas discharge tubes for Gemini 4 Argon and Neon.
In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon wrote a first-person WebGL2 freeride ski simulator from scratch on real Mont Blanc and Chamonix elevation terrain — combining 10,200 lines of custom shaders, 120 Hz ski physics across six alpine lines, dynamic carved tracks, slab avalanches, and spatial Web Audio with zero pre-made assets.
Using /swarm in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon pulled archival photos to recreate Alan Turing’s 1936 study at King’s College, Cambridge in interactive 3D — from King’s Chapel outside to Room X.8 inside, complete with a working Universal Turing Machine running on his desk.
In Google Antigravity, a Gemini 4 Neon agent swarm turned a single image into a 100,000-cell Google Sheet with zero embedded images and zero Apps Script — using over 500,000 live spreadsheet formulas to run edge detection, map 3D depth, and relight the scene across six interactive modes.
We’re refining thinking levels with each new model release to give teams finer control and a smoother progression from one tier to the next. Neon’s four levels scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to what each workload needs.
Neon delivers high performance at a lower cost per task across third-party benchmarks. At its default high thinking level, it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It also sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest engineering, analytical, and scientific workloads. Neon shows its highest intelligence score here, while still costing 36%+ less per task than competing models at their highest setting.
As agentic coding scales, generating secure code from the start is critical. Gemini 4 Neon for cyber produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench , achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%).
Securing systems also means proactively finding flaws before attackers do. Penetration testing has served as a cornerstone of enterprise cybersecurity. On WebExploitBench v1.2 , Neon is state-of-the-art (51.26%) at half the cost of competing large models.
To fortify existing code, Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost efficient than large frontier models.
Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the Fairwind Program .
Gemini 4 Neon builds on improvements from our Gemini 4 safety and security stack — maintaining Gemini 4 Carbon-level protections against severe misuse and prompt injection while advancing further on model alignment and agentic behavior. For a model meant to carry demanding, long-running work in production, we concentrated on:
In the Gemini app, Gemini 4 Neon excels at work that requires frontier-level reasoning and fast responses.
Neon is built for complex coding, analytical reasoning, and production-grade enterprise workflows. While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency. Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently.

TLDR: we project Gemini 4 Neon’s performance based on what a faster Gemini 4 Carbon might score and find it equivalent to Opus 5.5
Gemini 4 Carbon is the best model on the Agent Duel leaderboard if you exclude early voting. Carbon’s main problem is that it is slooooow .
Today, Gemini 4 Neon was released , and looks to be an incremental benchmark improvement with a very large speed improvement. Earlier today, it was being served extremely fast via OpenRouter: 127 tokens per second . This is way faster than Carbon at 46 tokens per second .
This got me wondering, could Neon be not just a good model but the best model?
To investigate, I modeled the win rate in our leaderboard. The best model has three components, model identity, speed and whether the user voted early. My initial modeling did poorly, so I added an interaction between speed and early voting. This ended up working well.
And surprisingly, speed seems to be pretty much as important as model identity (another blog on that soon).
If you assume the same performance as Gemini 4 Carbon (which is reasonable given even better benchmark scores), and 127 tps , we would project an Elo on the Agent Duel leaderboard of 1,066, just below Opus 5.5 at 1,078 in our later analysis snapshot.
The 90% interval for the projected Elo difference between Gemini 4 Neon and Opus 5.5 is -94 to +68, with Neon projected to win 48.3% of the time against Opus (counting ties as half a win).

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella weighed in on former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unexpected departure amid a series of shocking controversies .
“It’s all sort of pretty tragic in the sense of, you know, Jensen is somebody I’ve known for a long time. I’ve admired what he’s done, and at this point, I kind of want to give him space to figure this out,” Nadella said onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday.
Huang stepped down last week from his CEO role, which he has held for 33 years. Huang’s leadership has been central to Nvidia’s ascent to one of the world’s most valuable companies, but his judgment was questioned after it was reported that he had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy feeding information back to Beijing. It was also revealed that Huang was having affairs with two Nvidia employees, including one who was a direct report.
While the world waits to see what the long-term economic impacts of Huang’s departure might be, Nadella says he still has confidence in Nvidia, which is a close partner of Microsoft.
“I’ll just say this one thing,” Nadella added. “Colette [Kress, interim CEO at Nvidia] worked at Microsoft for a long time. I’ve known her for a long time. She’s a tremendous person… I’m in touch with the same set of people I was in touch with before [Huang left], so I have a lot of confidence in the Nvidia team and their ability to continue to do the good work.”
Microsoft is not unlike Nvidia in that its founder Bill Gates inhabited a larger-than-life persona as CEO.
“Founders are unbelievable in the sense that they create something from nothing, so that is pretty magical… They’re singular, but they’re not gods, right?” Nadella said. “I used to say to Bill [Gates]… Founders also die, and so at some point, a company, if it needs to succeed, it has to have someone take over.”
